raw_evidence.label: What surprised even the author: 60 ingredients in one cookie
raw_evidence.content: The most striking feature of the mathematical average isn't its proportions — it's its *length*. Because the mean is taken over the union of every ingredient that appears in any recipe, the average cookie contains roughly 60 ingredients, including trace quantities of bourbon (0.019 tbsp), applesauce (0.002 cups), zucchini (0.010 cup), espresso, coriander, marshmallows, and crispy rice. O'Brien kept these micro-quantities 'for science.' This is the corpus's hidden long tail: the median home baker uses about 8-10 ingredients, but the union across 211 recipes runs into dozens. This is the most blog-worthy interpretive hook — averaging a population of recipes does not produce the median recipe, it produces a Frankenstein superset. Yet the cookie tastes fine: 'Chewy and very chocolatey, no one would suspect these cookies were made with everything in your pantry.'

raw_evidence.label: How the average was computed
raw_evidence.content: O'Brien used three approaches in parallel and baked the result of each. (1) Mathematical Averaging: take every recipe scaled to 48 cookies, compute the mean quantity for each ingredient that ever appears, and use a sentence-vector cluster of the directions to pick a representative set of instructions. This produces the headline 'average' recipe. (2) N-gram predictive text: a 4-gram model that predicts the next word in a recipe based on word frequencies, generating a recipe one word at a time. The first attempt fell into an endless loop on a single recipe containing cannelini beans (no, really — that recipe had to be removed). (3) Character-level neural network: a deep model trained letter-by-letter that produced surrealist outputs like '1.904 cups seconds' and obsessively repeated white sugar five times across one ingredient list. The clean comparison shows that 'averaging' is not one method but a family of methods — and only the mathematical mean produced something edible.

raw_evidence.content: The most striking feature of the mathematical average isn't its proportions — it's its *length*. raw_evidence.label: How the average was computed
raw_evidence.content: O'Brien used three approaches in parallel and baked the result of each. (1) Mathematical Averaging: take every recipe scaled to 48 cookies, compute the mean quantity for each ingredient that ever appears, and use a sentence-vector cluster of the directions to pick a representative set of instructions. This produces the headline 'average' recipe. (2) N-gram predictive text: a 4-gram model that predicts the next word in a recipe based on word frequencies, generating a recipe one word at a time. The first attempt fell into an endless loop on a single recipe containing cannelini beans (no, really — that recipe had to be removed). (3) Character-level neural network: a deep model trained letter-by-letter that produced surrealist outputs like '1.904 cups seconds' and obsessively repeated white sugar five times across one ingredient list. The clean comparison shows that 'averaging' is not one method but a family of methods — and only the mathematical mean produced something edible.

raw_evidence.label: Background: the chocolate chip cookie recipe canon
raw_evidence.content: The chocolate chip cookie was invented by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Whitman, Massachusetts around 1938. Her 'Toll House Crunch Cookie' recipe appeared in the 1938 edition of *Tried and True*. Nestle bought the rights to print the recipe on every bag of chocolate chips, which is why a single 'canonical' recipe — flour, butter, white sugar, brown sugar, eggs, vanilla, baking soda, salt, and chocolate chips — has been copied, tweaked, and re-uploaded by tens of thousands of home bakers ever since. This is why a corpus of 211 internet recipes is unusually homogeneous compared to almost any other dish: the variation is mostly in proportions, not in ingredient identity. That homogeneity is what makes 'averaging' even possible here. Bread, by contrast, has hundreds of distinct variants; chocolate chip cookies, almost one.

raw_evidence.label: Background: the chocolate chip cookie recipe canon
raw_evidence.content: The chocolate chip cookie was invented by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Whitman, Massachusetts around 1938. Her 'Toll House Crunch Cookie' recipe appeared in the 1938 edition of *Tried and True*. Nestle bought the rights to print the recipe on every bag of chocolate chips, which is why a single 'canonical' recipe — flour, butter, white sugar, brown sugar, eggs, vanilla, baking soda, salt, and chocolate chips — has been copied, tweaked, and re-uploaded by tens of thousands of home bakers ever since. This is why a corpus of 211 internet recipes is unusually homogeneous compared to almost any other dish: the variation is mostly in proportions, not in ingredient identity. That homogeneity is what makes 'averaging' even possible here. Bread, by contrast, has hundreds of distinct variants; chocolate chip cookies, almost one.

# --- ana_15: Most common bigrams in directions (cooking verbs/phrases) ---

def tokenize(s):

toks = tokenize(text)
print(f"Total tokens (alphabetic): {len(toks)}")
print(f"Unique tokens: {len(set(toks))}")
bigrams = Counter(zip(toks, toks[1:]))
common_bigrams = bigrams.most_common(25)

for (a, b), c in common_bigrams:

raw_evidence.label: Background: the chocolate chip cookie recipe canon
raw_evidence.content: The chocolate chip cookie was invented by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Whitman, Massachusetts around 1938. Her 'Toll House Crunch Cookie' recipe appeared in the 1938 edition of *Tried and True*. Nestle bought the rights to print the recipe on every bag of chocolate chips, which is why a single 'canonical' recipe — flour, butter, white sugar, brown sugar, eggs, vanilla, baking soda, salt, and chocolate chips — has been copied, tweaked, and re-uploaded by tens of thousands of home bakers ever since. This is why a corpus of 211 internet recipes is unusually homogeneous compared to almost any other dish: the variation is mostly in proportions, not in ingredient identity. That homogeneity is what makes 'averaging' even possible here. Bread, by contrast, has hundreds of distinct variants; chocolate chip cookies, almost one.

sentences.summary: det_05: Why this matters: averaging vs. preferring. Source: Baking the Most Average Chocolate Chip Cookie (https://pudding.cool/2018/05/cookies/) Facts: Essay is positioned as a playful demonstration of automated recipe generation methods; Three computer-generated recipes were physically baked and judged | det_03: How the average was computed. Source: Baking the Most Average Chocolate Chip Cookie (https://pudding.cool/2018/05/cookies/) Facts: Three algorithms: mathematical mean, n-gram predictive text, character-level neural network; N-gram model entered an endless loop on a recipe containing cannelini beans

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: averaging vs. preferring
raw_evidence.content: Beyond the cookie itself, the essay is a small argument about machine-learning style 'recommendation by average'. Algorithms that recommend films, songs, or news articles often optimize toward the average preference of a population — which, like the average cookie, can include trace amounts of every minority taste, mush them together, and call the result a representative output. The cookie experiment makes the failure mode tactile: average is not the same as typical, and it is definitely not the same as good. The mathematical-average cookie is technically edible. The neural-network cookie is gibberish. The n-gram cookie loops on cannelini beans. None of them are what a person would actually call their favorite chocolate chip cookie.

sources.title: Baking the Most Average Chocolate Chip Cookie
facts: Essay is positioned as a playful demonstration of automated recipe generation methods
Three computer-generated recipes were physically baked and judged

raw_evidence.label: How the average was computed
raw_evidence.content: O'Brien used three approaches in parallel and baked the result of each. (1) Mathematical Averaging: take every recipe scaled to 48 cookies, compute the mean quantity for each ingredient that ever appears, and use a sentence-vector cluster of the directions to pick a representative set of instructions. This produces the headline 'average' recipe. (2) N-gram predictive text: a 4-gram model that predicts the next word in a recipe based on word frequencies, generating a recipe one word at a time. The first attempt fell into an endless loop on a single recipe containing cannelini beans (no, really — that recipe had to be removed). (3) Character-level neural network: a deep model trained letter-by-letter that produced surrealist outputs like '1.904 cups seconds' and obsessively repeated white sugar five times across one ingredient list. The clean comparison shows that 'averaging' is not one method but a family of methods — and only the mathematical mean produced something edible.

raw_evidence.label: The average cookie has 68 ingredients in trace amounts
raw_evidence.content: Because 'mean quantity' takes the union of every ingredient that appears in any recipe, the strict mathematical average has 68 distinct ingredients — the entire corpus vocabulary. 10 of them have a mean above 0.5 of their unit; 46 have a mean above 0.01; 19 are 'trace' ingredients with population means under 0.01. This is the joke at the centre of O'Brien's essay: an average is not a typical recipe. The average cookie technically contains a microgram of bourbon (0.019 tablespoons across 209 recipes), a smear of zucchini, and a homeopathic dust of coriander.

(1) Mathematical Averaging: take every recipe scaled to 48 cookies, compute the mean quantity for each ingredient that ever appears, and use a sentence-vector cluster of the directions to pick a representative set of instructions. This produces the headline 'average' recipe. (2) N-gram predictive text: a 4-gram model that predicts the next word in a recipe based on word frequencies, generating a recipe one word at a time. The first attempt fell into an endless loop on a single recipe containing cannelini beans (no, really — that recipe had to be removed). (3) Character-level neural network: a deep model trained letter-by-letter that produced surrealist outputs like '1.904 cups seconds' and obsessively repeated white sugar five times across one ingredient list. The clean comparison shows that 'averaging' is not one method but a family of methods — and only the mathematical mean produced something edible.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: averaging vs. preferring
raw_evidence.content: Beyond the cookie itself, the essay is a small argument about machine-learning style 'recommendation by average'. Algorithms that recommend films, songs, or news articles often optimize toward the average preference of a population — which, like the average cookie, can include trace amounts of every minority taste, mush them together, and call the result a representative output. The cookie experiment makes the failure mode tactile: average is not the same as typical, and it is definitely not the same as good. The mathematical-average cookie is technically edible. The neural-network cookie is gibberish. The n-gram cookie loops on cannelini beans. None of them are what a person would actually call their favorite chocolate chip cookie.
